content: Angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors are a class of medications that work by inhibiting the activity of the angiotensin-converting enzyme, which is responsible for converting angiotensin I into angiotensin II. Angiotensin II is a potent vasoconstrictor and plays a key role in regulating blood pressure and fluid balance. By blocking this conversion, ACE inhibitors reduce the production of angiotensin II, leading to vasodilation, decreased blood pressure, and reduced workload on the heart. Overview of ACE Inhibitors Specific drugs in this class include captopril, enalapril, and lisinopril. These medications are commonly used to treat conditions such as hypertension and congestive heart failure (CHF). Mechanism of Action Angiotensin is formed both systemically and locally in autocrine and paracrine systems. Local angiotensin systems have been identified in blood vessels, the heart, adrenal glands, kidneys, and brain. The conversion of angiotensinogen to angiotensin I is mediated by renin, which is the rate-limiting enzyme in this process. Angiotensin I, a decapeptide, is then converted into angiotensin II, an octapeptide, by the angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE). ACE inhibitors act on both systemic and local renin-angiotensin systems. In addition to promoting the synthesis of angiotensin II, ACE also facilitates the degradation of bradykinin, a potent vasodilator. By inhibiting ACE, these drugs increase bradykinin levels, which enhances the conversion of arachidonic acid to prostaglandins, further promoting vasodilation. This increase in bradykinin and prostaglandin synthesis may explain the common side effect of cough associated with ACE inhibitors. Use in Hypertension In patients with renal artery stenosis, reduced kidney perfusion leads to increased renin release by the juxtaglomerular apparatus. ACE inhibitors block the synthesis of angiotensin II in this hyperreninemic state. In patients without renal artery stenosis, ACE inhibitors lower blood pressure through several mechanisms: 1. Inhibition of the conversion of circulating angiotensin I to angiotensin II. 2. Reduction in aldosterone secretion, leading to natriuresis. 3. Induction of renal vasodilation, enhancing natriuresis. 4. Reduction in the inactivation of vasodilatory bradykinins. 5. Inhibition of local angiotensin II formation in vascular tissue and myocardium. 6. Indirect modulation of adrenergic activity. ACE inhibitors are considered to have a favorable side-effect profile and may improve quality of life compared to other antihypertensive agents. However, comparative studies often excluded cough as a side effect and used medications with central and sexual side effects, such as methyldopa and propranolol, for comparison. Use in Congestive Heart Failure (CHF) In CHF, a vicious cycle occurs where reduced cardiac output decreases baroreceptor stimulation, leading to increased systemic vascular resistance (SVR) and further increasing the afterload on the failing myocardium. ACE inhibitors reduce SVR and minimize afterload, thereby improving cardiac function. Additionally, patients with CHF are at risk for ventricular arrhythmias (VEA), and ACE inhibitors may provide benefit by increasing serum potassium levels and reducing circulating norepinephrine levels. However, more studies are needed to confirm these effects. In patients with liver dysfunction, captopril may be preferred over enalapril, as enalapril requires activation in the liver. Diuretics remain the first-line agents in CHF, and ACE inhibitors are typically used as second-line agents, as they are less effective in the absence of diuretics. Patients with hyponatremia (serum sodium <130 mEq/L) are likely to be hyperreninemic and may experience a significant drop in blood pressure with ACE inhibitors. Hyperkalemia should be avoided in patients already on potassium-sparing diuretics or potassium supplements, especially if renal function is impaired. Post-Infarction Remodeling Both experimental and clinical studies support the use of ACE inhibitors to reduce left ventricular (LV) dilation following myocardial infarction (MI). Use in Renal Impairment ACE inhibitors exert a renal vasodilatory effect by dilating efferent arterioles, thereby relieving intraglomerular pressure and reducing the filtered load. However, their role in other forms of renal failure is less clear. Captopril has been shown to improve proteinuria in diabetic nephropathy. Side Effects 1. Cough: A dry, irritating, non-productive cough is the most common side effect, occurring in up to 10-15% of patients. It is thought to be secondary to increased bradykinin and prostaglandin levels. NSAIDs may help alleviate the cough but may reduce the renal vasodilatory effects of ACE inhibitors. 2. Hypotension: In patients with very low initial blood pressure, further afterload reduction can cause hypotension and renal hypoperfusion. 3. Renal Side Effects: Hypotension can lead to renal failure, which is usually temporary. This is more likely in severe CHF, unilateral or bilateral renal artery stenosis. Occasionally, irreversible renal failure has been reported in patients with bilateral renal artery stenosis, making this a contraindication for ACE inhibitors. 4. Immune-Based Side Effects: Captopril, in particular, can cause taste disturbances (2-7%), skin rashes (4-10%), and neutropenia (1/8600). Regular white blood cell (WBC) monitoring is recommended in patients with renal impairment during the first three months of therapy. Drug Interactions 1. Avoid hyperkalemia with potassium-sparing agents. 2. Monitor plasma lithium levels when co-administered with ACE inhibitors. 3. Combination with thiazide diuretics enhances the hypotensive effects of ACE inhibitors. 4. Captopril increases digoxin levels. 5. ACE inhibitors and beta-blockers both reduce renin levels, and their effects may be additive. 6. ACE inhibitors and calcium channel blockers are a good combination as both are free of central nervous system (CNS) effects. Specific ACE Inhibitors 1. Captopril: The first ACE inhibitor with a short half-life (2-3 hours). It is dosed at 25-50 mg twice daily for hypertension and 75-150 mg daily in divided doses for CHF. It improves proteinuria in diabetic nephropathy but is contraindicated in bilateral renal artery stenosis, unilateral renal artery stenosis in a single kidney, and immune-based renal diseases. Immune-based side effects include taste disturbances, skin rashes, and neutropenia. WBC counts should be monitored in patients with renal impairment. 2. Enalapril: A pro-drug that requires activation in the liver. It has a longer half-life (4-5 hours in hypertension and 7-8 hours in CHF) and is 95% renally excreted. It is less likely to cause immune-based side effects compared to captopril. Regular neutrophil monitoring is not required. 3. Lisinopril: Not a pro-drug and is excreted unchanged by the kidneys. It has a longer half-life (12-14 hours) and fewer immune-based side effects. Its dosing is similar to enalapril. 4. Benazepril: A pro-drug hydrolyzed in the liver to its active form, benazeprilat. It is dosed at 10 mg once daily initially, with chronic dosing at 20-40 mg daily. Dose adjustments are required in patients with creatinine clearance <30 mL/min but not in cirrhosis or the elderly.
